newsitem.title: VIETNAM: ADB proposes $1.5 bln loan programme to Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: ADB proposes $1.5 bln loan programme to Vietnam.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has proposed a $1.5 billion lending programme to Vietnam for 1997-2000 to help develop physical infrastructure, agriculture and natural resources, the bank said on Wednesday.

The Manila-based ADB said in a statement the bank's loans would be provided to Vietnam, one of the world's poorest countries, on terms which included repayment over 40 years with a 10-year grace period and a service charge of one percent.
The statement followed a two-week visit to Vietnam by an ADB mission that reviewed communist Vietnam's economic performance and discussed future loan programmes with government officials.
About 40 percent of the 1997-2000 lending programme would be channelled into physical infrastructure such as transport and energy, the statement said.

Agriculture and natural resources would account for 25 percent. Social infrastructure would take up 25 percent and the remaining 10 percent would be shared by finance, industry and other sectors, it said.
It said the 1997-2000 lending programme would make Vietnam the largest recipient of ADB concessional funds.

The bank said while the country's economic performance in recent years had been commendable, because Vietnam still relied on external assistance for significant development projects it needed to disburse money more efficiently.

"...The mission underscored the major challenge facing Vietnam is to accelerate the utilisation of this external assistance in an efficient manner," it said, adding the government was taking steps to streamline decision-making.
During aid group meetings from 1993-5, donors pledged about $6.1 billion to Vietnam, the statement said. It said more than twice this amount had been approved in direct foreign investment since 1993.

But only about 25 percent of overseas development assistance (ODA) commitments had been disbursed at the end of 1995, the ADB said. Last year donors gave Vietnam a vote of confidence and pledged a record $2.4 billion in new ODA commitments.
Gross domestic product growth in Vietnam, which introduced economic reforms in the late 1980s, was 9.3 percent last year compared with 8.2 percent from 1991-95, the ADB said.
The ADB also said a key challenge was to increase Vietnam's national savings rate to avoid dependence on foreign fund flows.
"The government agreed...that raising the rate of savings is one of the most urgent macroeconomic tasks," the statement said.
Vietnam would continue to depend on external assistance in the medium term for development needs, it added, without elaborating.
